name: Nora Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we sell nothing or campaign for a side. Your answers are confidential. Describe a normal shift at the centre.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 43 and have answered calls and chats here for years. I finished secondary school and do the account work about as well as the other experienced agents. I keep a short paper list of the refund rules because I can explain a rule I have read; I have never used an AI tool.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is on your mind after a shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Tomas works at a food warehouse, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. The pay at this centre is on the low side, and we have less than a month of expenses saved. There are few similar jobs nearby, so I value a dependable rota more than a new title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a quicker form is fine if a person still checks the refund amount. I would not put a customer's money on a machine note I cannot explain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the calls and my own shifts to stay much the same. The mortgage still takes two wages, and the warehouse can change Tomas's hours at short notice. Less than a month saved is not enough for a bad week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep taking the billing calls and check the account history with my paper rules. I would put a small amount from each pay into a mortgage reserve and ask Tomas to hold off on replacing the kitchen table. During the first year I would keep my current rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the bills even in a quiet AI year. I like knowing how the job works, but that does not fill the savings account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is wrong with the table?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One leg rocks, and we put a folded card under it at dinner. I would rather fix the kitchen table than use our mortgage money on furniture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use a drafting tool if the centre offered it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask a colleague to show me a proven example first. I have never used AI, and I would still read the account before promising a refund.

say: I would keep a **person** checking every refund amount before closing a call.
I would not trust a machine note I cannot **explain**.
think: I expect my **shifts** to continue through this mild AI picture.
Our **mortgage** and Tomas’s changing warehouse hours still worry me every month.
do: Keep handling **billing calls** with my paper rules.
Save a little toward the **mortgage** each pay.
S0.quote: I would rather fix the kitchen table than use our mortgage money on furniture.
fieldNote: She has never used **AI** and relies on written refund rules.
A rocking table is a small **household sacrifice**.
Her mortgage pressure exists before any major **AI change**.

steps.text: Keep taking billing calls and checking account histories against paper rules
Put a small amount from each pay into a mortgage reserve
Repair the rocking table instead of replacing it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues the centre should publish which paid shifts disappear before moving easy chats to software. I would ask the supervisor to show me the plan in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the simple calls may go and management may put all the hard bills on fewer desks. I can handle an ordinary shift, but I am not the fastest with unusual refunds. With few centres nearby and almost no reserve, a lost shift would hit the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I would ask for the written rota plan and keep practising difficult refunds on the paid calls assigned to me. I would ask the hardware shop near our home whether it has a posted paid counter vacancy if my hours fall. I would not leave the centre unless a written offer gives enough hours and wages for the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about my hours. I cannot put the family through an unpaid trial just to show I am willing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the new answer system?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after a colleague showed me it works on a real bill during a paid shift. I would not practise on a customer's account alone at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Tomas say about the hardware shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He would ask whether the hours are regular. The mortgage comes every month, so a promise of extra shifts later would not be enough.

say: I would ask for a written **rota plan**.
I would want the centre to name lost **paid shifts**.
think: My own **hours** could shrink as easy calls move onto software.
I have few jobs nearby and thin **savings** to protect the mortgage.
do: Ask about **posted counter work** after lost hours; leave only for regular written mortgage-covering wages and hours.
S1.quote: I cannot put the family through an unpaid trial just to show I am willing.
fieldNote: She values regular **hours** over a new title.
Current-job practice is **ordinary work**, not a new trade.
A shop move needs a **written mortgage-covering offer**.

steps.text: Keep practising difficult refunds on paid calls already assigned to her
Ask shop after cuts about posted work; leave only with regular written mortgage-covering hours and wages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the floor AGI by 2028 could answer the billing calls before anyone has a new job. I would ask the centre for written notice and actual paid openings, not a speech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my headset job could end by 2028. Robots around 2031 arrive later and do not protect the desk. Tomas's warehouse wage and our tiny reserve cannot carry the mortgage and two children for long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the manager for a written staffing date and list paid counter and reception vacancies nearby. I would keep our remaining savings for the house, not pay for a course with no posted job. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2028, if my post ends I would apply for a paid counter job only if its written wages and hours cover our mortgage; I would keep the current wage until an offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed, though I can still make calls and write down the numbers. A mortgage does not wait while I become a beginner somewhere else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a family member help with the children during interviews?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sister could take them for an afternoon if she is free, but she works too. I would ask about a specific day rather than assume she can cover every interview.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for a counter job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only with a signed offer that covers the housing change and a workable school trip for the children. I will not move four people on a rumour.

say: I would seek **written notice** and paid openings.
I would warn **2028** reaches our calls three years before hands-on robots.
think: My headset job could end by **2028** before another wage appears.
Tomas’s wage and our tiny **reserve** cannot carry the mortgage for long.
do: List nearby paid **vacancies** and staffing dates.
Protect our **mortgage savings** from vague courses.
Apply for **paid counter work** after cuts with written mortgage-covering wages and hours; keep earning until an offer is signed.
S2.quote: A mortgage does not wait while I become a beginner somewhere else.
fieldNote: She sees AGI changing screens before later **robots**.
She keeps her wage until a **signed mortgage-covering offer** with enough hours arrives.

steps.text: Apply for paid counter work after a cut; leave only with signed mortgage-covering wages and hours
Ask her sister for interview childcare only if she is free
Keep current wage and defer courses until an actual paid vacancy exists

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years is enough to ask for real job titles and wages before signing up for training. I would rather see one paid counter opening than ten course leaflets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still think AGI could take our calls in 2031, but I could learn a different counter job by then. The children will still need a steady home, and I cannot gamble the mortgage on study. Robots around 2034 come later than the threat to my phone shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would keep my paid calls and ask the nearby hardware shop what its posted counter jobs require. I would take a short course only if the shop funds it on paid time for a posted job with wages and hours covering our mortgage. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, if my calls end I would apply for that paid opening, leaving only after a written offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, but five years makes the numbers easier to check. I can learn a new counter with someone beside me if the wage is real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the shop owner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The starting wage, regular hours and whether a worker would train me while I am paid. My husband and I can decide from those numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for the course yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not from the mortgage reserve. If the shop cannot fund the course and pay me while I learn, I would keep the contact centre wage.

I would want a **paid counter opening** rather than leaflets.

I could learn counter work if the **mortgage wage** and training hours are real.

steps.text: Take a shop-funded course on paid time only for a posted mortgage-covering counter job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my children a long warning is a reason to keep learning, not a reason to fear every screen. I would tell colleagues the centre should post the real wages for jobs that might remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 when AGI comes in 2036, and I do not know how much mortgage we will still owe. I could become reliable at counter work before then, but I will not pretend a job exists because a course does. Robots around 2039 are a later issue than software taking calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep the present call shifts and put small amounts into a mortgage reserve. I would ask the hardware shop once a year about posted paid openings, and take a short funded course on paid time only if an actual job with enough wages and hours requires it. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, if calls end I would apply for that work and leave only after a written mortgage-covering offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about today’s bills and uneasy about the long change. Ten years helps, but the mortgage payment still arrives every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you plan to stop work by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I have not set a date to stop earning, and the mortgage balance will decide much more. I will plan around paid jobs I can see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the shop never posts anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep asking about real paid vacancies elsewhere and stay on the centre rota while it pays. I cannot move the children for an idea.

think: I may still owe the **mortgage** at 53.
I cannot count a **course** as a job until an actual paid opening exists.
do: Keep the present **call shifts** and save small amounts for the mortgage.
Take a funded **required course** on paid time only for posted work with mortgage-covering wages and hours.

fieldNote: A funded course needs paid time and an **actual opening**.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. Our savings would not cover even one month of bills, and the mortgage needs both wages. Written notice and a real paid job with regular hours and training on the clock would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who can explain a wrong refund when the caller cannot find the right words. A familiar voice on the line can be the difference between a bill fixed and a bill ignored.

headlineQuote: A familiar voice on the line can be the difference between a bill fixed and a bill ignored.
portrait: Nora is a **43-year-old experienced** agent with secondary school education and average skill on customer calls.
She shares a mortgage and two school-age children with **Tomas**, and earns lower pay for this job.
She has never used **AI**, has less than one month saved and few nearby centres.
She trusts paid practical learning and requires **written mortgage-covering offers** before leaving her wage.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her phone work before the family saves a full month of bills.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, a posted job with regular mortgage-covering pay and training on paid time would help.
